Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim

Commentary on Surat al-Qiyamah

It is Meccan.

It is related from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "Whoever wishes to witness the Resurrection, let him recite Surat al-Qiyamah."

It is related from al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah that he said: "They say 'al-Qiyamah' (the Resurrection), but whoever dies, his resurrection has already come about."

Al-Naqqash cited these two reports in his tafsir.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said its meaning is: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection."

Also from him: he asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His words: ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾, and he said: "Indeed our Lord, exalted is He, swears by whatever He wills of His creation."

The scholars differed concerning His words "lā" (nay), and there are several opinions. One opinion is that it is ṣilah (a redundant particle, zaʾidah beyond what is the established usage of the Arabic language). Al-Farraʾ rejected this and said: "ṣilah occurs only in the midst of a speech, but not at its beginning." The meaning of ﴿lā﴾ is that the matter is not as they claim, that there is no resurrection, no Paradise and no Fire; then he began with His words ﴿I swear﴾. Those who held the first opinion replied that the whole Qur'an is connected, part to part, in meaning, so "lā" may be a ṣilah in this connecting position even though it occurs at the beginning of the surah.

The third opinion is that the meaning of ﴿lā﴾ is to alert (tanbih), as if he said: "Take heed (alā), then I swear." Similar to it is the verse of the poet:

(Alā wa-abīki ibnata al-ʿĀmirī... lā yaddaʿī qawmun annī afirru)

Ibn Kathir recited: "La-uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamah" (with the lam of emphasis), and this is the recitation of al-Hasan and al-Aʿraj.

Some of the Basran grammarians rejected this recitation, claiming it was a grammatical error (laḥn), and they said: the nun (of emphasis) must be present when it is in this form. The sound position is the well-known recitation, and most readers follow it.

As for His words ﴿the Day of Resurrection﴾ (al-qiyamah): it was called al-qiyamah because people will stand (yaqumun) on this day for the reckoning and the recompense for their deeds.

And the Most High's saying: ﴿Nay, I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ means: I swear.

Al-Hasan reported that he said: He swears by the Day of Resurrection, and He did not swear by the self-reproaching soul.

The more correct view is that the oath is by both of them.

Regarding al-Lawwamah (the self-reproaching soul) there are several opinions. The first: it is the wicked soul that is blamed on the Day of Resurrection, so the meaning of al-lawwamah here is "the one blamed" according to this view.

The second view, which is the more correct: it is the believing soul that blames itself for the sins it commits.

Mujahid said: The believer blames himself for sins, while the disbeliever proceeds boldly and persistently in sins and does not reflect upon them.

It is also mentioned in the tafsir: there is no one but that he blames himself on the Day of Resurrection. If he was a doer of good, he blames himself that he did not increase and multiply his good deeds; and if he was a doer of evil, he blames himself that he did not desist from wrongdoing and sins.

Translation:

And His saying, ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ That is: We will not bring his bones back to life (so that We gather them) for resurrection after they have been scattered.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 4:

And His saying: ﴿Yes[, indeed]﴾ is the response to the oath, and upon it the oath falls.

And His saying: ﴿capable[s]﴾ means: Yes, [We will be able to] gather you, [being] capable.

It is also said: Yes, We will have power, [being] capable.

And His saying: ﴿that We are able to make even his fingertips﴾ means: upon the making even of his fingertips, which are the tips of the fingers, and in them are small bones. He singled them out for mention because, if He, exalted is He, is able to gather small bones, then He is even more able to gather the large ones and bring them back to life.

And it is reported from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿that We are able to make even his fingertips﴾, that [it means] We make his fingers like the hoof of a camel and the hoof of a donkey. This is a well-known opinion in the books of tafsir.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 5:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Nay, but man desires to continue in sin before him﴾. In the tafsir it is said that its meaning is: he advances sin and postpones repentance.

This carries the sense of procrastination in abandoning sins and in turning back to Allah in repentance.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talha al-Walibi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that its meaning is: it is denial of the Resurrection. Fujur (transgression, from the root f-j-r, meaning to deviate or break from the proper course) is the inclination away from the truth, and the liar is inclined away from truthfulness, so he is a fajir (transgressor).

Ibn Qutayba related that a Bedouin came to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "My camel has become sore-backed, so carry me on another camel." ʿUmar did not carry him. The Bedouin turned away saying:

(I swear by Allah, Abu Hafs ʿUmar...
that no wound or sore-back has touched him)

(O Allah, forgive him if he has lied...)

That is, "he lied" (kadhaba).

Mujahid said regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿continue in sin before him﴾, that it means: he goes on ahead of himself, riding his desire, not reflecting on a sin, and not repenting of an act of disobedience.

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ That is: when is the Day of Resurrection? They would say this in a spirit of mockery, and this is evidence for the correctness of the view we mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾. It is also recited as "baraqa" (with a fatḥah on the ba'), so His saying "baraqa al-baṣar" means: the sight became fixed from terror, so it did not blink.

And His saying "baraqa" means: he became bewildered and distressed. It is also said: it overcame him like lightning (al-barq).

And His saying: ﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾, meaning: its light is gone.

From this it is said: a well that has caved in (munkhasifah) and one that has not caved in.

It is related from Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris al-Razi that he said: al-kusuf is when part of the light goes away, and al-khusuf is when all of the light goes away.

This is also a view transmitted from others besides him.

And His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾, i.e., in the eclipse and the removal of light.

Ibn Mas'ud said: They will become like two yoked camels, then they will be thrown into the Fire and become a fire upon the disbelievers, and this is in the sense of His saying.

And from Mujahid: ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾, i.e., both of them will be wound up (kuwwira).

And His saying: ﴿On that Day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ That is: where is the place of flight? It was also recited as "Where is the abode?" (al-maqarr), that is: where is the place of settling?

Its statement, ﴿Nay! There is no refuge﴾ means: there is no escape and no fleeing.

As for His statement, ﴿There is no refuge﴾, there are several views. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: there is no escape (muhays).

ʿIkrimah said: there is no protection (man'ah).

Regarding Mujahid: there is no place of deliverance (manjā).

Mutarrif ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir and al-Dahhak said: there is no mountain.

This is a well-known view. The Arabs, when horsemen attacked them, would say: "al-wizr, al-wizr!", meaning: "the mountain, the mountain!"

The poet said:

(By your life, there is no refuge for the youth, when death overtakes him and old age.)

And this is according to the meaning of "a place of deliverance" (manjā).

Its meaning: "To your Lord, that Day, is the place of rest" — that is, the place where the servants will settle becomes manifest, whether in Paradise or in the Fire.

Note on the translation: the Qur'anic quotation is rendered as "To your Lord, that Day, is the place of rest" and the commentary sentence follows it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 13:

And His saying: ﴿Man will be informed on that Day of what he sent forward and kept back.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: [what he sent forward] is an act of obedience which he performed, and [what he kept back] is a good practice (sunnah) or an evil practice (sayyi'ah) which he performed and which others acted upon after him.

It is also said: ﴿what he sent forward and kept back﴾ refers to the beginning and the end of his deeds.

This is related from Mujahid and Ibrahim.

It has also been said: ﴿what he sent forward and kept back﴾ means: he will receive the recompense for all his deeds, whether obedience or disobedience.

And it is related from Zayd ibn Aslam: [what he sent forward] is the wealth given in charity, and [what he kept back] is the wealth left for the heirs.

And His words: ﴿Nay, man will be a witness against himself﴾ — meaning, a witness (shahid). The sense is that the proof is binding upon him, just as it is established by testimony, and there is no one who does not have, from his own self, a proof against his own self.

It has also been said: it is the testimony of the limbs against him on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: his hands, his feet, his private parts, and other things will testify against him.

The tāʾ (ta marbuta) entered the word ﴿baṣīra﴾ for emphasis (mubalagha), like their saying ʿallama (one who knows much), riwaya (one who narrates much), and what resembles them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 15:

As for His saying: ﴿Even if he should offer his excuses﴾, there are two well-known opinions regarding it. The first: even if he were to come with every excuse and present every argument, i.e., it would not be accepted from him, because he has no excuse and no argument.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿Even if he should offer his excuses﴾ means his curtains (sutur), its singular being mi'dhar (مِعْذار). Al-Zajjaj said: it means the covering (al-satr).

It was also said: it is a Yemeni dialect (lughah yamaniyyah).

The meaning is: even if he covers all his deeds with curtains, they will nevertheless become manifest on the Day of Resurrection, and he will be recompensed for them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾ Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah related, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'isha, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to move his tongue with it when the revelation came down to him, wishing to memorize it, so God, the Exalted, revealed His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾ He said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr moved his lips, and Ibn 'Abbas moved his lips. He (may God be pleased with him) said: Abu 'Ali al-Shafi'i informed us of this hadith, Abu al-Hasan ibn (Firas) informed us, Abu Ja'far al-Dibuli informed us, Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi informed us, from Ibn 'Uyaynah.

The hadith.

There is a difference of opinion regarding why the Prophet used to move his tongue. One of the two views, which is the well-known one, is that he moved it out of fear of it slipping away, so that he would not forget it.

The second view is that he moved his tongue out of love for the revelation; this was related by al-Dahhak.

Wa qawluhu: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ means: its collection in your breast.

And "qur'anahu" means: We will make its recitation easy for you; so al-Qur'an here carries the meaning of qira'ah (recitation).

Qatadah said: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ means: its collection in your breast and its arrangement as We have sent it down.

And His saying: ﴿So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾ means: when We have sent it down, then listen to it.

It is also said: when Jibril recites it to you, then follow its recitation. And it has been said: "then follow its recitation" means: then follow the Qur'an by acting upon it, in what is lawful (halal) and unlawful (haram), and in its commands and prohibitions.

And His saying: ﴿Then indeed it is upon Us to make it clear﴾, meaning: it is upon Us to gather it in your breast so that you may make it clear to the people and recite it to them. This is mentioned in the sense of facilitating its memorization and making it easy for him, with the help of Allah the Exalted. He had previously encountered hardship in memorizing it, but when Allah the Exalted revealed this verse, whenever Jibril recited it to him, he would lower his head, and when [Jibril] had gone, he would recite it just as it had been revealed.

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty (life of this world) and neglect the Hereafter﴾. It is addressed to the disbelievers, because they used to work for the world and did not work for the Hereafter. This is the meaning of the verse.

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty (life of this world) and neglect the Hereafter﴾. It is addressed to the disbelievers, because they used to work for the world and did not work for the Hereafter. This is the meaning of the verse.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 75, verses 22–23:

His saying: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾. His saying: ﴿radiant﴾ with the ḍād, meaning: joyful, cheerful, bright of countenance and welcoming.

Al-naḍra (radiance) is, in the language, blessing and delight.

His saying: ﴿looking toward their Lord﴾ is the gazing upon Allah, Exalted is He, with the eyes. It is established for the believers in Paradise by the promise of Allah, Exalted is He, and by the report of the Messenger.

He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Abu al-Ḥasan ibn al-Naqqur informed us, Abu al-Qasim ibn Ḥabbaba informed us, al-Baghawi informed us, Hudba [ibn] Khalid informed us, from Ḥammad ibn Salama, from Thabit al-Bunani, from ʿAbd al-Raḥman ibn Abi Layla, from Ṣuhayb, from the Prophet, who said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, Allah, Exalted is He, says: 'Do you want anything more that I should give you?' They say: 'Have You not brightened our faces? Have You not admitted us into Paradise and saved us from the Fire?' He said: Then the veil is lifted, and they are given nothing more beloved to them than gazing upon Allah, Exalted is He."

He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Abu ʿAli al-Shafiʿi informed us in Mecca, Abu al-Ḥasan ibn Firas informed us with his chain, from Isra'il, from Thuwayr ibn Abi Fakhita, from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet said: "Indeed the lowest in rank among the people of Paradise is one who looks over his kingdom for a thousand years and sees its farthest end as he sees its nearest. And indeed the highest in rank among them is one who looks upon Allah, Exalted is He, twice every day."

And in another narration: "morning and evening." Then he recited His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant﴾.

What we have mentioned concerning gazing upon Allah is the view of the majority of the exegetes. It is also transmitted from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣri that he understood the verse in this sense, and all the narrators have mentioned it.

Some have reported from Mujahid: "looking toward the reward of their Lord." This is not sound, because the Arabs do not use this expression in such a context except to mean gazing with the eye. Perhaps the view attributed to Mujahid is not established, since no one whose narration can be trusted has transmitted it.

Some have interpreted His saying ﴿looking﴾ to mean "awaiting." This interpretation is also false, because the Arabs do not connect the word "looking" (nāẓira) with the particle "ilā" (toward) except with the meaning of gazing with the eye. The poet said:

(I looked at her from al-Muhassab in Mina... and I have a look, were it not for restraint, a fierce one)

But when they intend "waiting," they do not connect it with "ilā." The poet said:

(So indeed, if you two wait for me a moment... of time, it would benefit me with Umm Jundub)

That is, "wait for me." And in meaning this interpretation is also not sound, because joy, cheerfulness and delight arise only from reaching the sought-after object; but with waiting there is no such thing, for in waiting there is distress and hardship.

And His saying: ﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾, i.e., scowling and frowning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 25:

And His saying: ﴿Thinking that a calamity is to be inflicted upon them﴾, meaning: they are certain that the one who inflicts upon them a fāqirah (a calamity that breaks the back) is... 

Let me correct that and give the faithful translation:

And His saying: ﴿Thinking that a calamity is to be inflicted upon them﴾, meaning: they are certain that what is done to them is a fāqirah (a calamity), and the fāqirah is the severe matter by which the spine of the back is broken.

And it has been said: fāqirah means: destructive (wāhiyah), or a great matter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 26:

The saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Nay! When it reaches the collarbones﴾. The meaning: the matter is not as they suppose and imagine, and (they) use that when the soul reaches the collarbones (al-tarāqī).

Al-tarāqī is the plural of tarqūwa (collarbone), and it is the front of the throat connected to the chest, and it is the place of the death rattle (al-ḥashraja). This was mentioned by Abū ʿĪsā.

And [it is said]: ﴿Who is a healer?﴾ That is, is there a physician who can cure and treat? Qatadah said this.

It is also said that its meaning is: the angels say, "Who will ascend with his soul?" That is, will the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment ascend with it?

And His saying: ﴿And he will think that it is the parting﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "wa-ayqana annahu al-firaq" (and he was certain that it was the parting).

This is authentically related from him, and it is the meaning.

And His saying: ﴿And the leg is entwined with the leg﴾ means: the severity of this world is joined to the severity of the Hereafter.

It is also said: the anguish of death and the terror of the moment of departure gather upon him.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: It concerns a great matter. People prepare his body, and the angels prepare his soul.

From al-Ḥasan: "And the leg is entwined with the leg" means: in the shroud, and the leg here is the well-known leg. According to the first opinion, however, "the leg" carries the meaning of severity.

We have mentioned this before.

Translation of the passage:

And His saying: ﴿To your Lord, that Day, is the driving﴾ (al-masaq). It means: al-suq (the driving), for he will be driven either to Paradise or to the Fire by the command of God, exalted is He.

The Qur'an, 75:31: ﴿So he neither affirmed [the truth] nor prayed﴾. Its meaning: the disbeliever neither affirmed [the truth] nor prayed; he did not affirm and did not pray.

The commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on surah 75, verse 32:

His saying: ﴿But he denied and turned away﴾ means: he denied the signs of Allah, and turned away from the truth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 33:

And His saying: ﴿Then he went back to his family, swaggering﴾, meaning: strutting proudly.

The gait of al-Muṭayṭā (a mincing, strutting walk) is the gait of arrogant swaggering.

It was said: it is that he bends his back (yuwalli maṭāhu), and al-maṭā is the back.

In some tafsirs it is said: it is the gait of the Banu Makhzum.

It was also said: al-tamaṭṭī (swaggering) is stretching oneself out from laziness or sickness. As for stretching from sickness, it is not blameworthy; but as for stretching from laziness, when it is sluggishness in turning away from the truth, then it is blameworthy.

.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verses 34–35:

And His saying: ﴿Woe to you, and woe again!﴾ Scholars have differed regarding this expression. One view is that its meaning is: "Woe to you, then woe to you."

The second view is that its meaning is: "May what you dislike befall you, and draw near to you." This is the view of Qatadah and a group of others.

The third view is: "Blame is due to you (awlā laka)," and then the word for blame was dropped because it is not needed and because it is understood. This was mentioned by ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā.

In the tafsir (it is reported) that the Prophet (ﷺ) met Abu Jahl as he was coming out of the gate of the Banu Makhzum, strutting. He took him by the hand and shook him once or twice, then said to him: "Woe to you, and woe again!" So Allah the Exalted informed of the Prophet's words in the Qur'an as he had said them. This is a good view, because awlā in the language of the Arabs carries the meaning of "nearly" (kāda), and the word kāda is more fitting for the creation. So it is a report from Allah the Exalted of the words of the Messenger.

And they cited for the word awlā the verse of al-Khansa:

(I resolved to overcome some of my cares, so woe to my self, woe to it)
(I will drive my self onward with its state, whether it is for it or against it)

Āla means: state (ḥāla).

Almighty God's words: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ That is: left without being commanded or forbidden.

This was said by Mujahid.

It was also said: he will not be resurrected, nor called to account, nor punished. The poet said:

(So I swear by God with the utmost oath... that God has left nothing unattended.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 37:

And His saying: ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ It is also recited with the letter tā' (ta): "tumnā" (تمنى).

Al-Muni (المني) is a known fluid from which the human being is created. So the recitation with yā' (ya) refers to al-mani (المني), and the recitation with tā' refers to its meaning, which is the nutfah (النطفة, a drop of fluid).

And His saying: ﴿yumnā﴾ means: it is ejected into the womb.

It is also said: it is decreed.

The poet said:

(مَا يمنى لَك الماني ... )

That is: what the decreer decrees for you, the decree.

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on Surah 75, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then he was a clinging clot﴾, meaning: the sperm became a clinging clot, which is coagulated blood.

And his saying: ﴿Then He created [him] and proportioned [him]﴾, meaning: He created the human being from it and proportioned his creation.
And His saying: ﴿So He made of it two kinds, the male and the female﴾. It is said: from the semen (al-mani), [comes] the male and the female.

And His saying: ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾ Its meaning: Is not God, who created man from a drop of semen, able to give life to the dead? That is, He is able.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that whenever he reached this verse he would say: "Allahumma bala" (O God, yes).

In another narration: "Subhanaka, bala" (Glory be to You, yes).

This has also been related with a traced-back chain to the Prophet (ﷺ) in some of the musnads.

And God knows best and is most wise.
